title: U.S.-Iran Deal 'Closer Than Ever' as Pakistan Mediates Final Text
summary: A potential breakthrough in one of the world's most volatile rivalries emerged Friday, as Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif declared that a 'final, agreed upon text of the peace deal has been reached' between the United States and Iran. The announcement came hours after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said an agreement had 'never been closer,' and former President Donald Trump reposted the statement, suggesting a signing could occur within days. The flurry of diplomacy follows two days of direct strikes between the two nations this week, threatening to unravel a fragile pause in hostilities that began in April. Sharif said Pakistan is 'working closely with both sides to finalize the next steps.' Trump, on his Truth Social platform, outlined the broad contours: 'significant' sanctions relief and unfreezing of Iranian assets in exchange for Iran dismantling its nuclear program and handing over enriched uranium. The deal would be a memorandum of understanding, with technical negotiations to follow. However, obstacles remain. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the text is in 'final stages of summarising' but must circulate through multiple leadership bodies—including the army, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, parliament, and ultimately Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei—before consensus is reached. Al Jazeera's Tehran correspondent noted this process could be lengthy. Trump, meanwhile, accused Iran of leaking false details to state media and claimed Iran privately apologized. The White House has emphasized that any agreement would include 'performance-based components': verifiable dismantlement, disposal of enriched uranium, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and an end to support for regional proxies. As negotiations intensify, the world watches a diplomatic dance that could reshape Middle Eastern security—or collapse under the weight of mistrust.
why_it_matters: If a deal holds, it could lower the risk of a broader Middle East war and stabilize global energy prices — something that directly affects your family's cost of living and the safety of international travel. If it fails, the region could slide back into military strikes, with worldwide economic fallout.

background_read: The United States and Iran have had no formal diplomatic relations since 1980, when the U.S. Embassy in Tehran was seized and American hostages held for 444 days.
Iran's nuclear program has been a flashpoint for decades. A 2015 agreement (JCPOA) limited Iran's uranium enrichment, but the U.S. withdrew under President Trump in 2018, reimposing heavy sanctions.
Pakistan, a nuclear-armed neighbor of Iran, has previously acted as a mediator in regional conflicts, though its ties to both Washington and Tehran are complex.
The Strait of Hormuz, where about one-fifth of the world's oil passes, has been a site of tension; any disruption could spike global energy prices immediately.
Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei (Iran's highest political and religious authority since 1989) holds ultimate power over state matters, including any nuclear deal.

perspectives.description: Advocates argue that sanctions relief paired with verifiable dismantlement would be a historic breakthrough, reducing the chance of nuclear escalation. Iran's economy could recover, and regional tensions might ease, benefiting ordinary Iranians and global markets.

Critics warn that Iran cannot be trusted to fully dismantle its program; past cheating and the involvement of hardliners in the Revolutionary Guard make enforcement unreliable. Some say unfreezing assets only funds Iran's proxy wars and ballistic missile programs.

This mirrors past cycles: outreach, partial agreements, breakdowns. The involvement of Pakistan as a mediator is notable but adds another layer of competing interests. The real determinant will be the internal power struggle in Tehran among factions that see any deal either as a lifeline or a trap.

If a memorandum is signed, technical negotiations could take years, with constant threats of collapse. A formal agreement might reshape the balance of power in the Middle East, encouraging other non-nuclear arrangements. Conversely, failure could trigger a new arms race and direct military involvement from more countries.
